paras: The Sim McCoy raid was a reported attack by the "Hatfield gang" on the home of Sim McCoy, a brother of Randall McCoy, in Wyoming County, West Virginia, on a Saturday night in mid-January 1888. According to dispatches from Charleston and Parkersburg, the raiders tied Mrs. McCoy to a tree and shot her, killed a son, and burned McCoy, and by some accounts two young children, in the house. Papers across the country printed it as a new chapter of the Hatfield-McCoy feud, but every account was relayed from word reaching other towns, and the deaths of the children were never confirmed.

The reports placed the raid within the Hatfield-McCoy feud on the West Virginia-Kentucky line. A New York version of the story recalled that around the new year the Hatfields had surrounded and burned Randall McCoy's house across the Kentucky line, killing his wife, son and daughter, and that a McCoy raid into West Virginia followed in which three of the Hatfield party were killed. The Big Sandy News of Louisa, Kentucky, wrote that the Hatfields, "run out of Logan county by the Pikeville party," had then turned on "another McCoy family" in neighboring Wyoming County.

The first full version, a Charleston dispatch of January 18 carried by the Cincinnati Telegram, said word had come from Oceana that the gang raided Sim McCoy's house on Saturday night. The raiders blindfolded Mrs. McCoy, tied her to a tree and shot her together with her eldest son, then set the house on fire, and McCoy and his two youngest children burned to death. The New York version added that the family was "completely surprised," that the son was "tied up and riddled with bullets," and that McCoy barricaded a back room and resisted before the house was fired.

A different account from Parkersburg, dated January 21, called the victim Simon McCoy and said the band overpowered him and took his wife and "a mere boy" into the woods. There she was tied to a tree and fired at "for a time" until the leader ordered her killed, and the boy was killed as well. Meanwhile the rest of the party piled combustibles around the house and fired it; McCoy begged for his life from an upstairs window, was answered with a volley, and died in the flames, and his charred body was found in the ruins.

The Parkersburg dispatch reported that "the people are demanding that something be done by the Governor." The New York version had offered its details as all that had "yet been received," and no later report of arrests, an inquest, or confirmation from Wyoming County appears in the coverage.

The story spread by wire within days, from the Waterbury Evening Democrat in Connecticut on January 18 to the Evening Star in Washington and the Rock Island Argus in Illinois on January 19. By January 20 it had reached the Richmond Dispatch, the Savannah Morning News and the Wheeling Intelligencer, and the Parkersburg version was still running in Kansas on January 26. Headlines stressed the toll and the cruelty: "Five More McCoys Killed," "Devilish Hatfield Atrocity" over "Her Husband and Children Roasted," and "Five Persons Murdered by the Hatfield Gang."

Most papers printed the dispatch as settled fact, the Richmond Dispatch calling it "Another Bloody Chapter in the History of Extermination" and the Big Sandy News heading its copy "Keeping It Up." Only the Parkersburg account hedged, calling the children's deaths "not confirmed," and it alone said this branch of the family "had no connection with the feud" and that the attack was "unwarranted." Copying errors crept in as well: the Rock Island Argus named the victim "Sam McCoy," and the Wheeling Intelligencer had the gang tie "Mrs. Randall" to the tree.

Accounts differed on when and where the raid took place: most said Saturday night in Wyoming County, but the earliest item, datelined Oceana on January 18, put the house "in Pite County" and the raid "yesterday." They also differed on the dead, with the wire versions counting five, the Oceana item naming the "two eldest children" among the killed, and the Parkersburg dispatch treating only the wife, a boy and McCoy as certain.

reader.title: Sim McCoy raid
bases: Reported as a feud raid in which the 'Hatfield gang' killed members of one McCoy household at their home (A2, A6, A17); it targeted one family rather than a community, and no paper gives a racial element.

Every version is secondhand 'word' or 'information' reaching Charleston, Cincinnati or Parkersburg from Oceana (A1, A2, A17); the Parkersburg dispatch is a separate text but cites no separate source, hedges on the children (A17), and no local report, confirmation, arrest or inquest was found.

accounts.label: Charleston/Oceana wire (Cincinnati Telegram)
accounts.gist: Word from Oceana that the Hatfield gang raided Sim McCoy's house Saturday night, shot Mrs. McCoy at a tree with her eldest son, and burned McCoy and two youngest children in the house.

accounts.label: New York version of a Charleston special
accounts.gist: Five McCoys killed; the family was surprised, the son 'riddled with bullets', and McCoy made 'a weak defence' of a barricaded back room before the house was fired; offered as all details yet received.

accounts.label: Oceana item, Jan. 18
accounts.gist: Places the house in 'Pite County' and the raid 'yesterday', with the two eldest children killed besides the wife.

accounts.label: Parkersburg dispatch, Jan. 21
accounts.gist: Simon McCoy, uninvolved in the feud, was overpowered; his wife and a boy were shot in the woods on the leader's order and he died in his burning house; the children's deaths unconfirmed.

framing.detail: Headlines called it 'Devilish Hatfield Atrocity', 'A Terrible Crime' and 'Brutal Outrages', and the Parkersburg text called the attack 'unwarranted'.
Most papers ran the Charleston or Cincinnati wire copy unchanged as a further chapter of the feud, e.g. 'Five More McCoys Killed'.
The Big Sandy News of Louisa, Ky., headed it 'Keeping It Up' and framed it as the Hatfields' 'work of annihilation' after being driven from Logan County.

conflicts.note: Most versions say Saturday night; the single 'yesterday' item is the earliest but the shortest.
